source.title: Unveiling Language-Specific Features in Large Language Models via Sparse Autoencoders
source.authors: Boyi Deng; Yu Wan; Yidan Zhang; Baosong Yang; Fuli Feng

record.tranche_reason: The study applies SAE-based feature analysis and interventions to multilingual LLMs, reporting results on whether SAE features capture language-specific properties in that setting.
record.gate_note: The study measures SAE feature activations and ablates SAE features, so those results bear on V4. Steering-vector task performance is not included as a row: it evaluates the authors’ proposed method rather than independently testing the claim about feature representations.
record.test_reason: The study uses pretrained Gemma Scope and Llama Scope SAEs as an analysis tool for multilingual mechanisms. It cites superposition only as motivation and never measures it. It does not test whether these models hold sparse features an SAE recovers: there is no comparison with neurons, no reconstruction or sparsity analysis, and no check of SAE fidelity. Its results describe language-specific directions, not superposition or dictionary recovery as such.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that some SAE features are strongly tied to specific languages and also track language context in code-switching. Ablating them mainly harms the corresponding language, and some languages have multiple synergistic features. They also claim that gating steering vectors on these features gives better language control (Table 1), which the paraphrase omits.
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes pretrained multilingual LLMs using SAE feature scoring, code-switching activation measurements, and directional ablation; it does not use the original toy-model setup.
record.method_sensitivity: Ablation effects vary across layers. The code-switching results also vary by noun language and layer; the paper reports a larger Spanish-prefix effect for French than Korean nouns.

fits_no_version.finding: Top-ν SAE directions are language-specific. Ablating the top-2 directions for a language raises CE loss mainly on that language, with large variation across layers, in Gemma 2 2B/9B and Llama-3.1-8B.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: LLMs contain linear directions selectively necessary for processing a specific language.

fits_no_version.finding: Jointly ablating the rank-1 and rank-2 French features raises French CE loss more than the individual ablations in some layers, and roughly additively for other languages.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Language-specific features interact non-additively within their own language.

fits_no_version.finding: A Spanish prefix raises Spanish-feature activation and lowers original-language feature activation on French and Korean nouns, more so at deeper layers and for French.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Language features encode linguistic context, not just token identity.

record.problems: The ablation and activation results are largely presented in figures without numerical values in the text; no uncertainty estimates are stated. The authors note that their experiments cover 10 languages but not some low-resource languages, and that the SAEs were not trained on curated multilingual data.
record.rows_left_out: The paper’s steering-vector task results were not cataloged because they evaluate the proposed steering method rather than independently testing the claim about SAE feature representations.

untested.parts: All: no toy models, sparsity sweep or geometry.
All: neurons are not analysed and there is no capacity manipulation.
Whether features are spread across neurons (no neuron analysis), and whether SAEs recover sparse features (taken as given; no reconstruction, sparsity or neuron-baseline comparison).
Completeness, stability and canonicality of SAE features. The text only notes that SAEs were not trained on multilingual data.

record.verdict_notes: The record's claim that the study tests V4 is not supported. Superposition appears only as a citation explaining why neurons are unreliable, and SAE validity is assumed. The ν-versus-random comparison is circular because features are selected by ν. The steering results are the authors' own method and correctly excluded.

versions.untested_parts: Toy networks, sparse features exceeding dimensions, overlap geometry, and sparsity-dependent transitions.
Whether polysemantic neurons result from capacity competition or important features receiving dedicated dimensions.
Whether polysemantic neurons arise for reasons other than capacity pressure.
The study analyzes SAE features, not whether features are spread across multiple neurons; it does not establish this as a general property of LLM representations.
Completeness, stability, and canonical status of SAE features.
Whether model features are intrinsically one-dimensional rather than multidimensional.

rows.subject: Gemma 2 2B
rows.operation_detail: Compared monolinguality scores for top-ranked SAE features with a random feature.
rows.measure: Feature monolinguality score ν across languages
rows.value: The paper states that the top-4 features have higher ν than the random feature; for most languages, rank #1 is considerably higher than the other top-ranked features.
rows.note: The figure reports language-by-language values; the text gives the qualitative comparison.
rows.check: Selection value. Top features are ranked by ν, so they beat a random feature by construction. This says nothing about superposition or whether the SAE recovers features.

source_check.problem: Selection statistic: features are ranked using this same score; this comparison is not an independent phenomenon result.

rows.value: The paper states that the top-ranked features show strong monolingual characteristics and that, in most scenarios, rank #1 suffices.
rows.note: Appendix text describes the plotted results as similar to Figure 1.
rows.check: Same selection circularity as R1 (Gemma 2 9B, Fig. 11). The comparison with a random feature follows from ranking on ν.

rows.subject: Gemma 2 2B
rows.operation_detail: Directional ablation of the top-2 language-specific features for each target language.

conditions.value: target-language texts versus texts in other languages

rows.baseline: CE loss before ablation; numerical baseline not stated
rows.value: Ablation has a much larger impact on target-language text CE loss than on other-language text CE loss; target-language changes vary significantly across layers.
rows.note: The paper reports the qualitative comparison in the text; the plotted values are not transcribed here.
rows.check: This shows that ablating the selected directions harms the target language most. That is a language-specificity result, not a measure of superposition or of whether an SAE recovers sparse features. No non-SAE direction control is used.

rows.subject: Gemma 2 2B
rows.operation_detail: Compared ablating French rank-1 and rank-2 features individually with ablating them together.
rows.baseline: CE loss without feature ablation; numerical baseline not stated
rows.value: For French, jointly ablating both features has a greater effect than individual ablations in some layers. For Spanish and Japanese, the joint effect is approximately the sum of the individual effects.
rows.note: The paper reports the synergistic effect only in some layers for French; Japanese effects are described as nearly zero across layers.
rows.check: The synergy of feature ablations is about interactions between language features, not any version's construct. The 'partial' state was graded against no relevant version.

rows.subject: Gemma 2 2B
rows.operation_detail: Measured a Spanish SAE feature’s activation on nouns with and without a Spanish prefix.
rows.measure: Mean activation of the Spanish feature
rows.baseline: Corresponding noun without a Spanish prefix
rows.value: A Spanish prefix raises the Spanish-feature activation for French and Korean nouns, but it remains below the activation for a Spanish prefix combined with a Spanish noun.
rows.note: The text also reports larger increases at deeper layers and a larger increase for French than Korean nouns.
rows.check: Code-switching context effects on a feature's activation do not bear on superposition or on SAE recovery.

rows.subject: Gemma 2 2B
rows.operation_detail: Measured French- and Korean-feature activations on corresponding nouns with and without a Spanish prefix.
rows.measure: Mean activation of the original-language feature
rows.baseline: Corresponding noun without a Spanish prefix
rows.value: For both French and Korean nouns, the original-language feature activation is lower with a Spanish prefix than when the noun stands alone.
rows.note: The text reports larger decreases at deeper layers and a larger decrease for French than Korean nouns.

relation.reason: Superposition motivates the choice of SAE analysis; the experiments test multilingual mechanisms and steering rather than a listed superposition claim.

tranche.reason: Uses pretrained SAEs to analyze language specificity and improve steering. The reported measurements concern language selectivity and intervention effects, without independently measuring superposition or sparse decomposition fidelity.

source_check.notes: R1–R3 are selection statistics and should not count as independent evidence. Ablation comparisons are qualitative; subsequent experiments focus on non-English languages.
